newsitem.title: KROATIEN: U.S. envoys join Balkan leaders at Split summit.
newsitem.headline: U.S. envoys join Balkan leaders at Split summit.

text.p: Richard Holbrooke, the straight-talking U.S. envoy who engineered Bosnia's peace agreement in 1995, arrived at a summit in Split on Wednesday to push Balkan leaders into speeding up the peace process.
He joined Croatian President Franjo Tudjman and the chairman of Bosnia's collective presidency, Alija Izetbegovic, at an old stone villa in the Adriatic port where they began a much-delayed summit.

They were expected to discuss Bosnia's Moslem-Croat Federation, which makes up half of the post-war country. Tudjman has faced international criticism for not supporting the federation, which was formed in 1994 with U.S. diplomacy.

"It's clear to me from what ambassador (Robert) Gelbard told me and from what I've observed, that progress is being made but at much too slow a pace," Holbrooke told Reuters Television after arriving at Split airport.
"We're here to encapsulate what has happened and try to accelerate the process and keep it moving forward," he added.
Wednesday's summit will provide Tudjman with his first opportunity to put into practice promises he made at his inauguration for a second term.
Taking the oath in Zagreb on Tuesday, he pledged to support both the 1995 Dayton peace accords and the Moslem-Croat Federation.
Yet he has been found wanting in his support of several aspects of Dayton, the agreement hammered out by Holbrooke during months of shuttling around former Yugoslavia.
The United States has led criticism of his failure to influence Bosnian Croat proteges who have refused to hand over suspected war criminals and have often undermined the Federation.

Gelbard, the current U.S. envoy to Bosnia, said he and Holbrooke "really are concerned that there has been a significant lag in implementation on the part of all the parties. We hope we can play a role in helping them achieve what they've committed themselves to achieve."
Izetbegovic, the Moslem chairman of the presidency, and Tudjman have had stormy relations ever since leading their republics to break away from the old Yugoslav federation.
Tudjman was anxious to hold the meeting earlier to prove to the United States and European governments that he was lending his support to the troubled Moslem-Croat Federation.

But Izetbegovic had declined to meet Tudjman for months until Zagreb made good on previous commitments. After coming under heavy Western pressure, Tudjman pushed the Bosnian Croats in Mostar into agreeing a unified police force last month.

"I solemnly declare that I shall be an impartial president of all Croats and Croatian citizens, regardless of their political and other affiliations," Tudjman said during his swearing in ceremony, implying that he considers Croats in other countries as his subjects. Many of them view him as their president.

Bosnian Croats living across the border from Croatia see themselves as Croatian citizens -- they vote in Croatian elections, their car licence plates are indistinguishable from Croatian plates and they use the Croatian flag and currency.
Croat-controlled towns in central Bosnia have begun allowing the return of Moslem refugees who were expelled during a 10-month Moslem-Croat war in 1993.

But over the weekend hundreds of Moslem refugees who had recently moved back to their pre-war homes around the Croat-controlled town of Jajce were forced to flee under intimidation and threats from angry, drunken Croat mobs.
There was no comment from Zagreb on the incidents.
